viewerChange.before: The intended viewer may see AI as a shortcut for starting or scaling a self-media account, including one-click generation of scripts or viral posts.
viewerChange.after: The intended viewer is pushed to distrust one-click AI promises, test promoters' incentives and results, prioritize human-selected topics and empathy, understand the author's claims about traffic variability and account weight, and restrict AI to supporting research gaps and brainstorming rather than substituting for authorship.
intendedChanges: Reconsider whether AI should be the primary author or growth engine for a self-media account.
Adopt a skeptical test for people selling AI agents, skills, or mini-programs.
Shift effort from buying a generator toward finding and writing a topic that reaches human concerns.
Treat viral performance as partly patterned yet not reliably reproducible.
Distinguish supporting uses of AI from one-click script generation.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: What is the contrarian opening promise, and what visual credibility signal precedes it?
observedSignals: A short inserted collage overlays the presenter and shows several large engagement/view counts plus the phrase 开头展示教资 as visually legible/near-legible text.
The masked presenter then states the absolute-sounding hook: do not use AI for self-media, account launching, or viral posts.
Burned captions highlight AI in yellow.
remainingUnknowns: The exact intended wording of the first SRT fragment 太多展示教资 is not resolved by machine transcription.
The source, platform, date, and attribution of the displayed metrics are not established.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: Who is warned away or invited in, and why does the author say promoters recommend AI?
observedSignals: The author limits the intended audience to people with dialectical/open logic and predicts conflict with AI users and AI-money peers.
The author asks who told the viewer to use AI and claims promoters want to sell agents, skills, and mini-programs to earn the viewer's money.
The presenter points at a prewritten whiteboard list while the setting remains continuous.
remainingUnknowns: No particular promoter, product, agent, skill, or mini-program is named.
The universal scope of the motive claim is not demonstrated.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: What two-case credibility test does the author apply to an AI promoter's profile?
observedSignals: Case one: if the promoter's own data are poor, the author says there is no reason to listen.
Case two: if the profile has high-performing posts, the author asserts those viral posts definitely were not made by AI.
The author broadens this into a universal claim about real bloggers not using AI for self-media.
remainingUnknowns: No profile is opened and no authorship audit is shown.
No empirical evidence establishes the absolute claims.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: What does the author call the activity closest to a viral post, and why is buying a one-click AI framed as a detour?
observedSignals: The author analogizes doing what is closest to money with doing what is closest to a viral post.
A good topic is named as the closest activity.
Buying an AI that promises one-click viral output is called nonsense because each account and IP needs concrete analysis and tailored training.
The presenter alternates between addressing camera and pointing to the whiteboard.
remainingUnknowns: No named AI, buying process, price, training method, or successful configuration is shown.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: How does the author connect topic selection, traffic uncertainty, and human empathy?
observedSignals: The author repeats that the nearest route is to find a topic that strikes deep human concerns and then write.
Traffic is described as having patterns that are themselves irregular; reposting the same viral item may not work because timing, place, and people matter.
Viral posts are said to be analyzable but sometimes not reproducible.
The author reframes content as human nature and content-making as empathy, calling machine-to-human empathy contemptuous.
remainingUnknowns: No comparative repost data or empathy test is shown.
The causal mechanism linking AI use to lack of empathy remains an author claim.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: Does the author literally reject all AI-made short video, or introduce a quality-threshold qualification?
observedSignals: The author says a 60-point video is not worth posting.
He explicitly says he is not declaring that AI cannot make short videos; AI can make short videos, but only 60-point ones in his framing.
For a novice trying to launch an account, that quality is called useless; for an established blogger, it is framed as even more dangerous because of weight.
remainingUnknowns: The scale and measurement behind 60 points are not defined.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: What numerical example explains the author's account-weight warning?
observedSignals: The author asks why some million-follower creators get only about one thousand likes.
His hypothetical baseline is a creator with one million followers and five ten-thousand likes for normal good content.
Several consecutive three-thousand-like videos are said to make the platform lower weight and base distribution, faster than for low-follower users.
The presenter draws/points to declining marks on the whiteboard.
remainingUnknowns: No platform documentation or observed account analytics prove the weight mechanism.
The number of weak posts required is only described as several.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: How does the author distinguish account launch from gradual accumulation and rebut the persistence story?
observedSignals: The author repeats that AI only makes 60-point videos and therefore should not be used to launch an account.
Account launch is framed not as slow accumulation but as overnight fame, with a drawn contrast between a gradual upward curve and a sudden jump.
The imagined persistence explanation is rejected; the breakthrough is attributed to the creator finally understanding how to make better content.
remainingUnknowns: No actual account trajectory or causal study is shown.
The strong overnight-fame claim remains an author claim rather than demonstrated fact.

carrierSweep.cognitiveQuestion: What AI uses survive the critique, what use remains prohibited, and how does the close reframe the opening?
observedSignals: AI is allowed as support for filling knowledge gaps during writing and for conversational brainstorming.
One-click generation of a script that is then directly filmed is explicitly prohibited.
The closing self-label conflicts across carriers: the burned caption reads 我是人类最强编导, while the supplied SRT and machine audio transcript read 我是人类智商编导; 下课 still reinforces a classroom/lesson persona.
The closing narrows the opening's absolute wording from do not use AI to do self-media into a distinction between assistance and substitution.
remainingUnknowns: The presenter's literal personal identity is not established.
No operational boundary is given for how much AI assistance is acceptable.
